---
title: "LIS: The Smallest Possible Tail for Each Length"
description: "Memorisable mathematical reasoning with small numerical examples."
---

## When to recognise the pattern

When you need the length of a longest increasing subsequence, not necessarily the subsequence itself.

## The key question

**Why does replacing a subsequence tail with a smaller value never hurt future extension?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
tail[k]=\min\{\text{last value of an increasing subsequence of length }k+1\}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** tail[k] is the smallest ending value among increasing subsequences of length k+1 encountered so far; k uses zero-based indexing; min chooses the least possible ending value.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Read [3,5,2,4]. After 3, tails=[3]. After 5, [3,5]. After 2, replace 3 with 2: [2,5]. After 4, replace 5 with 4: [2,4]. LIS length is 2 (for example 2,4 or 3,5).

## Why this is mathematically correct

A smaller tail for a given subsequence length is always at least as easy to extend with a future larger number as a greater tail. Keep only the best tail of each length; find replacement positions by binary search, giving O(n log n).

## Limits and counterexamples

The tails array is not necessarily an actual subsequence of the input. For strictly increasing LIS, replace the first tail ≥x; for nondecreasing LIS, use the first tail >x.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: For each length, keep the smallest ending value; smaller endings preserve every possible future extension.**

Now reproduce the equation, example and proof aloud, without looking.

**Interview problems:** Longest Increasing Subsequence; Russian Doll Envelopes.
